title: Agile & Distributed Teams
requirement: Led distributed/cross-functional engineering teams in agile environments.

questions.question: Which agile ceremonies do you keep valuable, and how do they change for distributed teams?
questions.answer: Planning sets a shared goal and an honest scope, standups surface blockers cheaply, reviews close the loop with stakeholders, and retrospectives fix process; those four carry the value. Distributed teams need them shorter and more structured, agendas in advance, cameras on, one conversation at a time, because silence over video hides the disengagement you would catch in a room. The async substitutes matter more than the meetings: a written standup and a recorded demo serve time zones that cannot attend live. A ceremony that produces no decision or artifact gets shortened or dropped; ritual without output is cost.
questions.keyTakeaway: Keep the four ceremonies short and decision-focused; cover time zones with async artifacts.

questions.question: How do you run estimation with a distributed cross-functional team?
questions.answer: Estimate in relative units, story points or t-shirt sizes, against a shared reference story, because hours invite false precision across skill levels. Async-first: stories are written and refined in the tracker before the session, so the meeting debates open questions instead of reading requirements aloud for the first time. Split anything the team cannot size in the room, because an unsizable story is an undefined story. Use the velocity trend for planning conversations only, never individual speed comparisons, or the numbers inflate instantly.
questions.keyTakeaway: Relative sizes against a reference, refinement before the meeting, split what cannot be sized.

questions.question: How do you keep a team effective when it spans multiple time zones?
questions.answer: Make written work the primary artifact: decisions, designs, and status live in documents and the tracker, so no one needs a meeting to be informed. Protect a small overlap window for the synchronous things that genuinely need it, decisions and unblocks, and let everything else run async with explicit response-time expectations. Rotate meeting times so the same region does not always take the 10 PM call, and record the decision meetings for the other half. Watch handoff quality, work handed across zones should arrive with context and acceptance criteria, or you buy rework with the time-zone savings.
questions.keyTakeaway: Documents over meetings, one protected overlap hour, fair rotation, context-rich handoffs.

questions.question: Velocity is down two sprints in a row. What do you do?
questions.answer: First look for cause, not blame: unplanned interrupt work, underestimated stories, review latency, on-call load, or a genuine staffing change each need different fixes. Pull the data, interrupt tickets, cycle time by stage, scope changes mid-sprint, and put it in front of the team, because the team usually knows the cause before the chart does. Fix the flow problem, protect focus time, kill a recurring interrupt source, tighten review turnaround, and let velocity recover on its own. What I never do is set velocity as a target, because teams will meet the number by inflating estimates and splitting nothing.
questions.keyTakeaway: Diagnose flow, not people; fix the interrupt source; never target the velocity number.

questions.question: Retrospectives keep happening but nothing changes. How do you fix that?
questions.answer: Cap the action list at one or two items, each with an owner and a due date, and start the next retro by reviewing those items before collecting new ones, which is the discipline most teams skip. Prefer process changes that are structural and cheap to keep, a new refinement checklist, an interrupt rotation, over promises that need willpower every day. Give changes two sprints before judging, and kill the ones that do not pay for their overhead, so the process stays honest. If actions keep dying because no one has time, the real retro topic is why the team has no slack.
questions.keyTakeaway: One owned action at a time, review it before new topics, and question the missing slack.

questions.question: A cross-functional dependency, design, data, or another team, blocks your sprint. How do you handle it?
questions.answer: Surface the dependency at planning with a name and a date, not a hope, because blockers discovered mid-sprint are planning failures. Work the interface directly: agree a contract or mock with the other team so both sides can build in parallel instead of waiting for the finished artifact. If the date slips twice, escalate with facts, what is blocked, the cost of the delay, the ask, to someone who can re-prioritize, and record the decision. Between sprints, feed the pattern back, chronic dependencies mean the team boundaries or the roadmap sequencing need redesign, not another escalation.
questions.keyTakeaway: Contract to unblock in parallel, escalate with cost and ask, then fix the boundary.
